questions.questionText: A word indicating 'Action' is called —
questions.explanation: A verb is a word that expresses an action, occurrence, or state of being.

questions.questionText: "You should dress for cold weather today." The word 'dress' is a —
questions.explanation: After a modal auxiliary (should), the following word is always a verb (base form).

questions.questionText: "I did the work." Here 'did' is a/an —
questions.explanation: When 'did' is the only verb in the sentence and carries full meaning, it is a principal verb.

questions.questionText: "She sleeps." Here the verb 'sleep' is a —
questions.explanation: Intransitive verbs do not take a direct object.

questions.questionText: The intransitive use of "She milks the cow" is —
questions.explanation: In quasi-passive, the original object becomes the subject with active form but passive meaning.

questions.questionText: "He went mad." The verb 'went' is —
questions.explanation: When 'go' is followed by an adjective (mad, bad, wild), it becomes a linking verb meaning 'become'.

questions.questionText: "He raised his hand." Here 'raised' is a —
questions.explanation: Causative verbs express that the subject causes someone/something else to do the action.

questions.questionText: Rafiq had Mizan ___ the floor.
questions.explanation: After 'have + person', always use the bare infinitive (base form) — no 'to'.

questions.questionText: The speaker failed to make the audience ___ to him patiently.
questions.explanation: After 'make + object' in active voice, always use bare infinitive — no 'to'.

questions.questionText: "She is a teacher." The word 'is' here is a —
questions.explanation: 'Is' connects the subject to its complement (teacher), so it is a linking verb.

questions.questionText: "They are playing football." The word 'are' here is a —
questions.explanation: 'Are' helps the main verb 'playing' — it is an auxiliary verb.

questions.questionText: "The milk turned sour." The verb 'turned' is a —
questions.explanation: 'Turned' connects 'milk' to 'sour' (adjective describing state) — linking verb.

questions.questionText: "She enjoys reading books." The word 'reading' is a —
questions.explanation: 'Reading' acts as a noun (object of 'enjoys') — it is a gerund.

questions.questionText: "The broken window needs repair." The word 'broken' is a —
questions.explanation: 'Broken' modifies the noun 'window' — it is a past participle used as adjective.

questions.questionText: "I saw him running." The word 'running' is a —
questions.explanation: 'Running' describes what 'him' was doing — present participle (part of participial phrase).

questions.questionText: "He is too tired to walk." The phrase 'to walk' is a —
questions.explanation: 'To walk' is the infinitive form of the verb.

questions.questionText: "Swimming is good exercise." The word 'Swimming' is a —
questions.explanation: 'Swimming' is the subject of the sentence — it functions as a noun (gerund).

questions.questionText: "She made me laugh." The verb 'laugh' is in —
questions.explanation: After 'made me', 'laugh' is in base form (bare infinitive without 'to').

questions.questionText: "I want to go home." The phrase 'to go' is a —
questions.explanation: 'To go' is the infinitive form — 'want' takes to-infinitive.

questions.questionText: "The running water was cold." The word 'running' is a —
questions.explanation: 'Running' modifies the noun 'water' — present participle used as adjective.

questions.questionText: "He doesn't have a car." The word 'have' is a —
questions.explanation: 'Have' here means 'possess' — it is a principal verb, not an auxiliary.

questions.questionText: "She has gone home." The word 'has' is a —
questions.explanation: 'Has' helps the main verb 'gone' — it is an auxiliary verb (present perfect tense).

questions.questionText: "The children are happy." The verb 'are' is a —
questions.explanation: 'Are' connects the subject 'children' to the adjective 'happy' — linking verb.

questions.questionText: "She seems tired." The verb 'seems' is a —
questions.explanation: 'Seems' connects the subject to its complement — linking verb.

questions.questionText: "He feels happy." The verb 'feels' is a —
questions.explanation: 'Feels' connects the subject to the adjective 'happy' — linking verb.

questions.questionText: "She became a doctor." The verb 'became' is a —
questions.explanation: 'Became' connects the subject to its complement — linking verb.

questions.questionText: "The door opened easily." The verb 'opened' is used —
questions.explanation: 'Opened' has no object — used intransitively (quasi-passive sense).

questions.questionText: "She had her hair cut." The phrase 'had her hair cut' is —
questions.explanation: 'Had + object + past participle' is a causative construction (she arranged for someone to cut it).

questions.questionText: "He let me go." The verb 'let' is a —
questions.explanation: 'Let' means to allow/cause someone to do something — causative verb.

questions.questionText: "They got the work done." The phrase 'got done' is —
questions.explanation: 'Got + object + past participle' is a causative construction.

questions.questionText: "She is reading a book." The word 'is' is a —
questions.explanation: 'Is' helps 'reading' form the present continuous tense — auxiliary verb.
